etymology: Hebrew Yesha’yāhū, “the LORD is salvation”; from yāsha’ (to save) and the divine name. The name is itself the gospel his book proclaims.
biblical_def: Isaiah the son of Amoz was the great evangelical prophet of Judah, ministering in Jerusalem through the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah in the eighth century before Christ. Called by a vision of the LORD high and lifted up, with the seraphim crying “Holy, holy, holy,” he was cleansed by the live coal from the altar and sent to a people whose ears were heavy and whose eyes were shut. No prophet sets forth the person and work of Christ more fully. He foretold the virgin’s Son, Immanuel; the child born and the Son given upon whose shoulder the government should rest; the Branch out of the stem of Jesse; and supremely the suffering Servant of chapter fifty-three, wounded for our transgressions and bruised for our iniquities, upon whom the LORD laid the iniquity of us all. He proclaimed the sovereignty of God over the nations, the folly of idols, the comfort of the gospel, and the new heavens and new earth. The dictionary receives the book as the work of one Isaiah, eighth-century, against the modern partition into a second and third hand. His witness is one unbroken testimony to the Holy One of Israel who is also the Redeemer.
webster_summary: An eighth-century prophet of Judah, son of Amoz; author of the prophecy bearing his name, foremost among the Old Testament witnesses to the coming and the atoning death of Christ.
webster_full: ISAIAH, n. [Hebrew, the LORD is salvation.] One of the greater prophets; a man of Judah who prophesied at Jerusalem under four kings.
Distinguished above the other prophets for the fulness, clearness, and evangelical sweetness of his predictions concerning the Messiah.
Called to his office by a vision of the LORD upon a throne, attended by the seraphim, and cleansed for service by a coal from the altar.
The author, by the testimony of the New Testament and the church, of the entire book of sixty-six chapters that bears his name.
Honored by the evangelists and apostles, who quote him more than any other prophet in setting forth the gospel of Christ.
scriptures: Isa 6:8
Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me.
Isa 7:14
Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.
Isa 53:5
But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
Isa 9:6

For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.
corruption_summary: Modern criticism dismembers Isaiah into several authors across centuries, denying that one prophet foresaw the Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning corruption is the so-called documentary partition of Isaiah—the claim that chapters forty through sixty-six were written by an anonymous “Second Isaiah” of the exile, and parts later still by a “Third Isaiah,” because no true prophet could have named Cyrus or comforted exiles generations before they were born. This rests not on the manuscript evidence, which knows one undivided book, but on the prior refusal to allow genuine predictive prophecy. The unbelief is in the premise, not in the text.

Scripture itself forecloses the partition. The Lord Jesus and the apostles quote freely from both halves of Isaiah and ascribe them to the one prophet, the Holy Ghost speaking by Isaiah. To divide the book is to make the LORD’s challenge empty—“shew the things that are to come hereafter, that we may know that ye are gods”—for it was precisely the foretelling of distant things that proved the living God against the idols. The dictionary holds one Isaiah, and one prophetic Spirit.
roots_summary: The name joins the verb to save with the covenant name of God, declaring salvation to be the LORD’s own work.
roots_lines: Hebrew yāsha’ — to save, deliver, give victory; the root behind both Isaiah and Joshua and Jesus.
Hebrew Yah — the shortened covenant name of the LORD, set at the end of the prophet’s name.
The full sense, “the LORD is salvation,” is the thesis of the whole book and the meaning of the gospel.
The same root yields yeshū’āh, salvation, the word Isaiah uses for the deliverance God brings.
Greek Esaias in the New Testament preserves the prophet’s name in the apostolic citations.
usage: Isaiah is read in Advent and Passion seasons because no prophet so clearly foretells the birth and the death of Christ.
Preachers turn to Isaiah fifty-three as the clearest Old Testament exposition of substitutionary atonement.
The threefold “Holy, holy, holy” of Isaiah six grounds the church’s confession of the holiness and the triunity of God.

etymology: Hebrew Mal’ākī, “my messenger”; from mal’āk (messenger, angel). The name befits the prophet who foretold the messenger of the covenant.
biblical_def: Malachi was the last of the writing prophets, raised up after the return from Babylon to rebuke a people grown cold in the days of the rebuilt temple. The priests despised the LORD’s name and offered the blind and the lame upon the altar; the men dealt treacherously against the wives of their youth and against the wife of the covenant; the people robbed God in tithes and offerings and wearied Him with their words, saying it was vain to serve Him. To this generation Malachi brought the word of a God who changes not, who still loved Jacob, and who would yet send His messenger to prepare the way before Him. He foretold the sun of righteousness arising with healing in His wings, the coming of Elijah before the great and dreadful day of the LORD, and the book of remembrance written for them that feared the LORD and thought upon His name. After Malachi the prophetic voice fell silent for four hundred years until John the Baptist came in the spirit and power of Elijah. The dictionary receives Malachi as the closing seal of the Old Testament and the hinge that opens upon the gospel.
webster_summary: The last of the Old Testament prophets, who after the exile rebuked a careless priesthood and people and foretold the forerunner and the coming of the Lord to His temple.
webster_full: MALACHI, n. [Hebrew, my messenger.] The last of the minor prophets, and the last prophetic voice before the four silent centuries.
A prophet of the restored community, who reproved the priests for polluted offerings and the people for treachery in marriage and robbery in tithes.
Foretold the messenger who should prepare the way of the Lord, fulfilled in John the Baptist.
Closed his prophecy and the Old Testament canon with the promise of Elijah before the day of the LORD.
His book stands as the bridge between the Testaments, the final word of the law and the prophets pointing to Christ.
scriptures: Mal 3:1

Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me: and the Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple, even the messenger of the covenant, whom ye delight in: behold, he shall come, saith the LORD of hosts.
Mal 3:6
For I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed.
Mal 4:2
But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings; and ye shall go forth, and grow up as calves of the stall.
Mal 3:10

Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it.
corruption_summary: The prophet’s witness to God’s unchanging covenant love is softened into a generic divine benevolence stripped of judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the immutability of God is the ground of the sinner’s safety: “I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed.” A modern sentiment that prizes a God who is endlessly flexible and accommodating loses the very rock on which Malachi stands; it is precisely because God does not change that His covenant holds and His threatened judgment is sure.

Where corruption does press in, it is in the handling of Malachi’s rebuke of treacherous divorce. “The LORD, the God of Israel, saith that he hateth putting away.” An age that has made marriage dissoluble at will would silence this word; the dictionary lets it stand. Malachi binds the covenant of marriage to the covenant of God, and the man who breaks the one shows his contempt for the other.
roots_summary: The name means “my messenger” and is taken up in the prophecy itself, which foretells the messenger of the covenant.
roots_lines: Hebrew mal’āk — messenger, envoy, angel; one sent with another’s word.
The suffix -ī — “my,” yielding “my messenger,” the LORD’s own envoy.
The word reappears in chapter three: “I will send my messenger,” fulfilled in John the Baptist.
mal’āk habberīth — “messenger of the covenant,” the title of the coming Lord Himself.
Greek angelos renders the same idea in the Septuagint and the New Testament: a sent one bearing a word.
usage: Malachi is read at Advent because the gospels open by quoting his promise of the forerunner.
The prophet’s “I change not” is a standard proof-text for the immutability of God.
Stewardship sermons appeal to Malachi’s charge against robbing God in tithes and offerings.

etymology: Hebrew Elīshā’, “my God is salvation”; from El (God) and yāsha’ (to save).
biblical_def: Elisha the son of Shaphat was the prophet who succeeded Elijah, called from the plough as he was breaking the twelfth yoke of oxen, and clothed with a double portion of his master’s spirit when Elijah was taken up in the whirlwind. He took up the fallen mantle, divided Jordan, and ministered in Israel through the reigns of several kings of the northern kingdom. His was a ministry crowded with mercy and with signs: he healed the bitter waters of Jericho with salt, multiplied the widow’s oil, raised the Shunammite’s son, healed Naaman the Syrian leper in the Jordan, made the iron axe-head swim, and fed a hundred men with twenty loaves. Many of these wonders prefigure the greater ministry of Christ, who cleansed lepers, raised the dead, and fed the multitudes. Elisha also saw the unseen armies of the LORD, the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire, and prayed that his servant’s eyes might be opened. He died of sickness, yet his very bones gave life to a dead man cast into his grave, a final witness that the God of resurrection was with him. The dictionary honors him as a true prophet of mercy in an apostate kingdom.
webster_summary: The prophet who succeeded Elijah, received a double portion of his spirit, and wrought many miracles of mercy in the northern kingdom, several of them foreshadowing the works of Christ.
webster_full: ELISHA, n. [Hebrew, my God is salvation.] The disciple and successor of Elijah in the prophetic office.
Called from following the plough, he left all and followed the prophet, ministering to him until his master’s ascension.
Endued with a double portion of Elijah’s spirit, he wrought more recorded miracles than any prophet before Christ.
His wonders—cleansing the leper, raising the dead, multiplying bread—stand as types of the works of the Lord Jesus.
A prophet to the apostate northern kingdom, he held forth the mercy of God amid the idolatry of the house of Ahab and Jehu.
scriptures: And it came to pass, when they were gone over, that Elijah said unto Elisha, Ask what I shall do for thee, before I be taken away from thee. And Elisha said, I pray thee, let a double portion of thy spirit be upon me.

And he took the mantle of Elijah that fell from him, and smote the waters, and said, Where is the LORD God of Elijah? and when he also had smitten the waters, they parted hither and thither: and Elisha went over.

And Elisha prayed, and said, LORD, I pray thee, open his eyes, that he may see. And the LORD opened the eyes of the young man; and he saw: and, behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha.
Then went he down, and dipped himself seven times in Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God: and his flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child, and he was clean.
corruption_summary: Rationalist readers strip Elisha’s miracles of their reality, reducing them to legend or folk-tale.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the God of Elisha is the living God who does wonders, and that His mercies in the prophet’s hand point forward to Christ. The cleansing of Naaman by sevenfold washing in Jordan is held up by the Lord Jesus Himself as a rebuke to unbelieving Israel and a sign of grace reaching the Gentile; to empty it of history is to lose its gospel.

Where modern handling errs, it is in the rationalist refusal of the miraculous—the assumption that the axe-head could not swim, the dead could not rise, and the chariots of fire were a poetic flourish. The dictionary receives the narrative as sober history. The same power that opened the servant’s eyes to the mountain full of horses and chariots is the power that raised Jesus from the dead, and the believer is taught by Elisha to reckon the unseen armies of God more real than the visible host of the enemy.
roots_summary: The name confesses that salvation belongs to God, a fitting banner over a ministry of delivering mercy.
roots_lines: Hebrew El — God, the Mighty One; the first element of the name.
Hebrew yāsha’ — to save, deliver; the same root that stands in Isaiah, Joshua, and Jesus.
Together: “my God is salvation,” a name nearly synonymous in sense with the name of the Saviour.
The doubled prophetic office—Elijah then Elisha—mirrors the law and the gospel, judgment and mercy.
Greek Elisaios preserves the name in the Septuagint and in our Lord’s reference in Luke four.
usage: Elisha’s miracles are preached as types of Christ’s healings and raisings.
The opening of the servant’s eyes is a standard text for the reality of the unseen warfare and the protection of God.
Naaman’s washing in Jordan is used to teach the simplicity and offense of the gospel’s appointed way.

etymology: Hebrew Ḥaggay, probably “festal” or “my feast,” from ḥag (a feast, a pilgrim festival).
biblical_def: Haggai was a prophet of the return from Babylon, raised up with Zechariah in the second year of Darius to stir the discouraged remnant to rebuild the house of the LORD. The people had laid the foundation years before, then let the work cease while they panelled their own houses and the temple lay waste. Haggai brought a sharp and timely word: “Consider your ways.” They had sown much and brought in little, eaten without being filled, and earned wages to put into a bag with holes, because they sought their own houses while God’s house lay desolate. At his preaching the governor Zerubbabel and the high priest Joshua and all the remnant obeyed the voice of the LORD, and the work went forward. Haggai promised that the glory of the latter house should exceed the former, for the Desire of all nations should come and fill it with glory—a word the church reads as fulfilled when Christ Himself entered the second temple. He further promised to shake the heavens and the earth and to make Zerubbabel as a signet, a pledge of the Messianic line. The dictionary honors Haggai as the prophet of priorities, who taught that the kingdom of God must be sought first.
webster_summary: A post-exilic prophet who, with Zechariah, roused the returned remnant to finish rebuilding the temple, and foretold that the Desire of all nations would fill the latter house with glory.
webster_full: HAGGAI, n. [Hebrew, festal.] One of the minor prophets, who prophesied after the return from the Babylonian captivity.
Sent in the second year of Darius to rebuke the people’s neglect of the LORD’s house while they dwelt in their own ceiled houses.
His brief prophecy of two chapters stirred Zerubbabel and Joshua to resume and complete the building of the second temple.
Foretold that the glory of the latter house should be greater than the former, fulfilled in the coming of Christ.
A prophet of right priorities, summoning the people to seek first the house and kingdom of God.
scriptures: Hag 1:4
Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your ceiled houses, and this house lie waste?
Hag 1:7
Thus saith the LORD of hosts; Consider your ways.
Hag 2:7
And I will shake all nations, and the desire of all nations shall come: and I will fill this house with glory, saith the LORD of hosts.
Hag 2:9
The glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former, saith the LORD of hosts: and in this place will I give peace, saith the LORD of hosts.
corruption_summary: The prophet’s call to put God’s house first is inverted by a religion that makes personal comfort the measure of blessing.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the ordering of loves: “Consider your ways.” Haggai diagnoses a people who prospered themselves and starved the worship of God, and who found their barns leaking and their wages vanishing under the curse. The lesson is not that God grudges His people houses, but that when His worship is set last, all else is set wrong, and that the kingdom of God must be sought first.

A subtler corruption misreads the promise “the desire of all nations shall come” as a flattering word about every nation’s religious longings being equally valid. Scripture means the Desire Himself, the Christ, the one for whom the true longing of the nations is satisfied. The latter house was made more glorious not by gold but by the presence of the incarnate Lord walking in its courts; the dictionary keeps the promise fixed on Him.
roots_summary: The name is bound to the festal joy of the pilgrim feasts, fitting for a prophet who called the people back to the house of worship.
roots_lines: Hebrew ḥag — a feast, a pilgrim festival kept at the appointed place of worship.
The name Ḥaggay — “festal” or “my feast,” perhaps marking birth on a feast day.
The festal root suits the prophet whose burden was the restoration of the temple and its worship.
Greek Aggaios renders the name in the Septuagint citations.
The same consonants underlie the regular Hebrew word for the great feasts of Israel’s calendar.
usage: Haggai’s “Consider your ways” is preached to call professing believers to examine their priorities.
The promise of the latter house’s greater glory is applied to the presence of Christ in His church.
Stewardship and building campaigns appeal to Haggai’s rebuke of neglecting the house of God.

etymology: Hebrew Mirām, of uncertain sense, perhaps “bitter” or “beloved”; the same name carried into Greek as Mariam and so into the New Testament as Mary.
biblical_def: Miriam was the sister of Moses and Aaron, the daughter of Amram and Jochebed of the tribe of Levi. As a girl she watched over the ark of bulrushes among the reeds of the Nile and wisely offered to fetch a Hebrew nurse for the infant Moses, so that his own mother was paid to raise him. After the crossing of the Red Sea she is called a prophetess, and she took a timbrel in her hand and led the women of Israel in the song of triumph, answering Moses’ song with the refrain, “Sing ye to the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously.” Yet she is also a warning. When she and Aaron spoke against Moses over the matter of his wife, jealous of his unique mediation, the anger of the LORD was kindled, and Miriam was struck with leprosy white as snow. Moses cried for her healing, and after seven days shut out of the camp she was received again. She died at Kadesh and was buried there. The dictionary remembers her both as a woman honored in the deliverance and song of Israel and as a solemn example that the LORD will vindicate His appointed servants against the murmuring even of their own kin.
webster_summary: The sister of Moses and Aaron, a prophetess who led Israel’s women in song after the Red Sea, and who was later struck with leprosy for speaking against Moses.
webster_full: MIRIAM, n. The elder sister of Moses and Aaron, of the tribe of Levi.
As a child she watched the ark of bulrushes and procured her own mother as nurse for the infant Moses.
Called a prophetess; she led the women of Israel with timbrels in the song of triumph at the Red Sea.
Smitten with leprosy for seven days when she and Aaron murmured against the prophet Moses.
Died and was buried at Kadesh; remembered among the deliverers God set over Israel in the exodus.
scriptures: And Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a timbrel in her hand; and all the women went out after her with timbrels and with dances.
And Miriam answered them, Sing ye to the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea.
Num 12:1
And Miriam and Aaron spake against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman whom he had married: for he had married an Ethiopian woman.
Mic 6:4
For I brought thee up out of the land of Egypt, and redeemed thee out of the house of servants; and I sent before thee Moses, Aaron, and Miriam.
corruption_summary: Miriam is conscripted as a banner for overturning the order God set in Israel, against the plain lesson of her chastening.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning corruption seizes upon Miriam’s title “prophetess” to argue that Scripture sanctions women in the ruling and teaching offices over men, and reads her complaint against Moses as a righteous bid for equal authority. The text says the opposite. When Miriam and Aaron challenged the singular mediation God had given Moses—“Hath the LORD indeed spoken only by Moses?”—the LORD came down, vindicated His servant, and struck Miriam with leprosy. The chapter is a divine rebuke of the very ambition the corruption celebrates.

The honest reading honors Miriam without unmaking the order of Scripture. God did use her, gift her, and name her among Israel’s deliverers through Micah; women prophesied in both Testaments. But the office of teaching elder and the headship of the home and church belong, by God’s appointment, to qualified men. Miriam’s leprosy is the standing answer to every attempt to make her the patroness of egalitarian revolt; the dictionary lets the warning stand beside the honor.
roots_summary: Her name, the Hebrew form of Mary, is of debated sense and was borne by many daughters of Israel down to the mother of our Lord.
roots_lines: Hebrew Mirām — the proper name, variously explained as “bitter,” “beloved,” or “rebellion.”
Some derive it from mārāh, to be bitter, recalling the bitterness of bondage in Egypt.
Others connect it with a root for “beloved” or “wished-for child.”
The Greek Mariam carries the name into the New Testament as Mary.
Thus the prophetess of the exodus and the virgin mother of Christ share one ancient Hebrew name.
usage: Miriam’s song at the sea is a model of corporate praise for God’s mighty acts of deliverance.
Numbers twelve is preached to warn against murmuring jealousy of God’s appointed leaders.
Her name is noted as the Hebrew original of Mary, the most common woman’s name in first-century Judea.

etymology: Hebrew Yēhū’, “the LORD is He” or “Jehovah is He”; the son of Hanani, distinct from Jehu king of Israel.
biblical_def: Jehu the son of Hanani was a prophet of the LORD in the days of the divided monarchy, not to be confused with the better-known Jehu who reigned as king of Israel. He was sent first against Baasha king of Israel, pronouncing the doom of that king’s house for following the sins of Jeroboam. Years later the same prophet met Jehoshaphat king of Judah as he returned in peace from the disastrous alliance with wicked Ahab, and rebuked him to his face: “Shouldest thou help the ungodly, and love them that hate the LORD? therefore is wrath upon thee from before the LORD.” Yet the prophet tempered the rebuke with grace, noting the good things found in Jehoshaphat, that he had taken away the groves and prepared his heart to seek God. Jehu is also named as the chronicler whose words concerning Jehoshaphat were entered into the book of the kings of Israel. The dictionary honors him as a faithful prophetic voice who feared neither king of the north nor king of the south, and who modeled the prophet’s duty to confront the unequal yoke of the righteous with the wicked.
webster_summary: A prophet, son of Hanani, who pronounced judgment on Baasha of Israel and rebuked Jehoshaphat of Judah for allying with ungodly Ahab; not the king of the same name.
webster_full: JEHU, n. [Hebrew, the LORD is He.] A prophet, the son of Hanani, in the era of the divided kingdom.
Sent against Baasha king of Israel to declare the destruction of his house for his idolatry.
Rebuked Jehoshaphat of Judah for joining himself in alliance and battle with the wicked king Ahab.
Recorded the acts of Jehoshaphat in the book of the kings of Israel.
To be distinguished from Jehu the son of Nimshi, the king who destroyed the house of Ahab.
scriptures: And Jehu the son of Hanani the seer went out to meet him, and said to king Jehoshaphat, Shouldest thou help the ungodly, and love them that hate the LORD? therefore is wrath upon thee from before the LORD.
Nevertheless there are good things found in thee, in that thou hast taken away the groves out of the land, and hast prepared thine heart to seek God.
And also by the hand of the prophet Jehu the son of Hanani came the word of the LORD against Baasha, and against his house, even for all the evil that he did in the sight of the LORD.
Now the rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, first and last, behold, they are written in the book of Jehu the son of Hanani, who is mentioned in the book of the kings of Israel.
corruption_summary: The prophet’s rebuke of the unequal yoke is dismissed by a tolerance that calls all alliances equally wise.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the prophet’s charge against the ungodly alliance: “Shouldest thou help the ungodly, and love them that hate the LORD?” Jehoshaphat was a good king, yet his marriage-alliance and military league with the house of Ahab brought wrath and nearly cost him his life. The lesson, carried into the New Testament’s “be ye not unequally yoked,” is that the friendship of the world is enmity with God, and that even a true believer may sin grievously by binding himself to the enemies of the LORD.

A second lesson is the balance of the prophet’s word. He did not flatter, but neither did he despair of a man in whom grace was at work; he named the good things found in Jehoshaphat in the same breath as the rebuke. Faithful correction tells the whole truth: it neither softens the sin to spare the feelings, nor denies the genuine fruit of grace to make the rebuke sharper.
roots_summary: His name confesses the LORD alone as God, the very point his prophecies pressed against idolatrous kings.
roots_lines: Hebrew Yēhū’ — commonly explained as “the LORD is He,” a confession of the true God.
The first element Yē — a form of the divine name Yah, the LORD.
The element hū’ — “he,” affirming the LORD as the very God.
Distinct from Jehu son of Nimshi, the king, who bore the same name.
His father’s name Hanani means “gracious,” from the root ḥanan, to show favor.
usage: Jehu son of Hanani is cited to warn against believers yoking themselves with the ungodly in alliance.
His balanced rebuke of Jehoshaphat is a model of faithful and gracious correction.
He is distinguished in study from Jehu the king to avoid confusing the two.

etymology: Hebrew Mēnashsheh, “causing to forget,” from nāshāh (to forget); the name first given by Joseph to his elder son, later borne by the long-reigning king of Judah.
biblical_def: Manasseh the son of Hezekiah was the longest-reigning king of Judah, fifty-five years upon the throne, and for most of them the most wicked. He undid his godly father’s reforms, rebuilt the high places, reared altars to Baal and the host of heaven in the very courts of the temple, made his sons pass through the fire, used enchantments and dealt with familiar spirits, and shed innocent blood very much, till he had filled Jerusalem from one end to another. By his idolatry he seduced Judah to do worse than the nations the LORD had destroyed before them, and his sin is named in Kings as the final cause of the captivity. Yet his account in Chronicles ends in astonishing mercy. The LORD brought the king of Assyria’s captains, who took Manasseh with hooks and bound him with fetters and carried him to Babylon. There, in his affliction, he besought the LORD and humbled himself greatly before the God of his fathers, and God was intreated of him and brought him again to Jerusalem. Then Manasseh knew that the LORD He was God, and he put away the strange gods and repaired the altar of the LORD. The dictionary holds him forth as the chief monument that no sinner is beyond the reach of sovereign grace.
webster_summary: The son of Hezekiah and most wicked of Judah’s kings, who reigned fifty-five years in idolatry and bloodshed, yet in captivity humbled himself and was restored—a signal trophy of grace.
webster_full: MANASSEH, n. [Hebrew, forgetting.] The son and successor of Hezekiah, king of Judah, and the longest-reigning of its monarchs.
Notorious for restoring idolatry, defiling the temple, practicing sorcery, and shedding innocent blood in great abundance.
Named in the second book of Kings as the king whose sins sealed the doom of Judah’s captivity.
Carried captive to Babylon, where he humbled himself, prayed, and was brought again to his kingdom.
In his restoration he put away the strange gods, a late and genuine repentance recorded in Chronicles.
scriptures: And he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD, after the abominations of the heathen, whom the LORD cast out before the children of Israel.
And when he was in affliction, he besought the LORD his God, and humbled himself greatly before the God of his fathers,
And prayed unto him: and he was intreated of him, and heard his supplication, and brought him again to Jerusalem into his kingdom. Then Manasseh knew that the LORD he was God.

Moreover Manasseh shed innocent blood very much, till he had filled Jerusalem from one end to another; beside his sin wherewith he made Judah to sin, in doing that which was evil in the sight of the LORD.
corruption_summary: Critics pit the two accounts of Manasseh against each other, denying the historicity of his repentance.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the reach of sovereign grace. If God could humble and convert the king who filled Jerusalem with innocent blood and led a nation into the deepest idolatry, then no sinner is too far gone for mercy when he humbles himself and seeks the LORD. Manasseh stands beside the dying thief and the persecutor Saul as proof that grace abounds over the chief of sinners.

Where modern handling errs, it is in the historical-critical claim that the Chronicler invented Manasseh’s repentance to solve a theological puzzle, since Kings records only his wickedness while Chronicles adds his conversion. The dictionary rejects the pretended contradiction. Kings records the public effect of his reign and the judgment it earned; Chronicles records the secret dealing of God with the man’s soul in captivity. Both are true: a converted sinner’s repentance does not erase the temporal consequences his sins set in motion.
roots_summary: The name “forgetting” is ironic in the king who forgot the LORD, then was made in mercy to remember Him.
roots_lines: Hebrew nāshāh — to forget, the root of the name Manasseh.
The name first given by Joseph: “God hath made me forget all my toil.”
In the king it reads as a sad omen—he forgot the God of his father Hezekiah.
In his restoration the irony turns to grace: he was made to remember that the LORD He was God.
The same name marks the half-tribe of Manasseh in Israel, descended from Joseph’s son.
usage: Manasseh is preached as the supreme Old Testament example that no sinner is beyond the reach of grace.
His reign is cited as the historical tipping point that sealed Judah’s exile in Kings.
The two accounts illustrate how genuine repentance may not remove the temporal fruit of past sin.

etymology: Hebrew Amōn, perhaps “faithful” or “master-workman,” though the king bore none of the faithfulness the name suggests; not to be confused with the Egyptian deity of similar spelling.
biblical_def: Amon the son of Manasseh was king of Judah for only two years, and those wholly evil. He came to the throne at twenty-two and walked in all the way of his father’s early wickedness, serving the idols that Manasseh had served and worshipping them, but unlike his father he did not humble himself before the LORD. Where Manasseh, after his fall, repented and was restored, Amon trespassed more and more and would not abase himself; he forsook the LORD God of his fathers and walked not in His way. His own servants conspired against him and slew him in his own house, and the people of the land then slew the conspirators and made his son Josiah king in his stead. So out of this dark and brief reign came the godly Josiah, who would lead Judah’s last great reformation. The dictionary marks Amon as a solemn warning of squandered example: he had before his eyes the proof of his father’s late mercy, yet he hardened himself and perished in his sin. The kindness that leads to repentance was despised, and judgment came swiftly.
webster_summary: A wicked king of Judah, son of Manasseh, who reigned but two years in idolatry without his father’s repentance, was slain by his servants, and was succeeded by godly Josiah.
webster_full: AMON, n. A king of Judah, the son and successor of Manasseh.
Reigned two years and did evil in the sight of the LORD, as his father had done in his wickedness.
Unlike Manasseh, he humbled not himself before the LORD, but trespassed more and more.
Was slain in a conspiracy of his own servants within his house.
The father of Josiah, the reforming king who turned to the LORD with all his heart.
scriptures: And he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD, as his father Manasseh did.
And humbled not himself before the LORD, as Manasseh his father had humbled himself; but Amon trespassed more and more.
And he forsook the LORD God of his fathers, and walked not in the way of the LORD.
Mat 1:10
And Hezekiah begat Manasses; and Manasses begat Amon; and Amon begat Josias;
corruption_summary: The hard reign of Amon is flattened into mere politics, missing the moral warning of grace despised.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the peril of despising a parent’s late repentance. Amon had the living testimony of his father Manasseh, the worst of sinners brought to humble himself and find mercy; yet Amon would not abase himself. He sinned against light, and his two short years ended in violent death. The contrast the Chronicler draws—Manasseh humbled himself, Amon humbled not himself—is the whole lesson: it is not the depth of past sin that damns, but the refusal to repent.

A second observation guards against political reductionism. Modern readings explain Amon’s murder and the people’s counter-vengeance as palace intrigue and dynastic maneuver, which historically it was; but the Chronicler reads the same events under the hand of God, who was preparing the throne for Josiah and Judah’s last reformation. The dictionary holds both: the LORD governs the conspiracies and counsels of men to accomplish His covenant purpose.
roots_summary: The name suggests faithfulness or skilled workmanship, a sense the king belied by his unrepentant idolatry.
roots_lines: Hebrew Amōn — the king’s name, perhaps from ’āman, to be firm, faithful.
The root ’āman also yields ’ēmūnāh, faithfulness, and our word “amen.”
By another derivation the name means “master-workman” or “skilled craftsman.”
The Hebrew king is wholly distinct from the Egyptian idol Amun of similar spelling.
In Matthew’s genealogy the Greek form Amōn places him in the line of Christ.
usage: Amon is preached as a warning to children of the godly who reject their parents’ repentance.
His reign illustrates that sinning against light hardens and hastens judgment.
He appears in Matthew’s genealogy as an ancestor in the royal line of Christ.

etymology: Hebrew Gabrī’ēl, “man of God” or “mighty one of God,” from geber (strong man) and El (God).
biblical_def: Gabriel is one of only two holy angels named in Scripture, the other being Michael. He stands in the presence of God and is sent forth to make known the LORD’s redemptive purposes at their great turning-points. In the book of Daniel he is sent twice to give the prophet understanding: to interpret the vision of the ram and the goat, and to deliver the prophecy of the seventy weeks that numbers the time to Messiah the Prince. In the gospel of Luke he appears again at the dawn of the New Testament, sent first to Zacharias in the temple to announce the birth of John the Baptist, and then to the virgin Mary in Nazareth to announce the conception of the Son of the Highest, declaring that with God nothing shall be impossible. Gabriel is thus the herald of the incarnation, the angel who carried heaven’s announcement of the coming of Christ. He is a creature, a ministering spirit, and never an object of worship; his glory is wholly in his errand. The dictionary honors Gabriel as a faithful messenger of God, while marking that the angels themselves desire to look into the gospel he announced, and that the church worships not the herald but the King whose advent he proclaimed.
webster_summary: One of the two holy angels named in Scripture; the heavenly messenger who interpreted Daniel’s visions and announced the births of John the Baptist and of Christ.
webster_full: GABRIEL, n. [Hebrew, man of God.] One of the chief angels, named in the books of Daniel and Luke.
Sent to Daniel to interpret the vision of the ram and goat and to reveal the seventy weeks.
Sent to Zacharias to foretell the birth of John the Baptist, the forerunner.
Sent to the virgin Mary to announce the conception and birth of the Lord Jesus Christ.
A created and ministering spirit, standing in the presence of God; not to be worshipped.
scriptures: Dan 9:21
Yea, whiles I was speaking in prayer, even the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the beginning, being caused to fly swiftly, touched me about the time of the evening oblation.
Luk 1:19
And the angel answering said unto him, I am Gabriel, that stand in the presence of God; and am sent to speak unto thee, and to shew thee these glad tidings.
Luk 1:26
And in the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God unto a city of Galilee, named Nazareth,
Luk 1:35

And the angel answered and said unto her, The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God.
corruption_summary: Popular religion exalts Gabriel into an object of devotion and invention, beyond the modest witness of Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning corruption multiplies and exalts the angels beyond their warrant. Roman devotion makes Gabriel a patron to be invoked; folk religion and later traditions assign him roles and revelations Scripture never gives, and a whole literature of angelic hierarchies and intercessions has grown up that the Bible knows nothing of. The dictionary keeps to the sober text: Gabriel is named only in Daniel and Luke, always as a sent messenger, never as an intercessor to be prayed to.

A modern corruption runs the other way, treating Gabriel as mere symbol or literary device and emptying the annunciation of its reality. Scripture presents him as a real holy spirit really sent, who really stood before Zacharias and Mary with words that came to pass. The proper response to such a messenger is neither devotion to the angel nor unbelief of his word, but worship of the God who sent him and faith in the Christ he announced. The angels themselves point away from themselves: “See thou do it not; worship God.”
roots_summary: His name binds human strength to God, fitting for the mighty one who stands in the divine presence to bear God’s word.
roots_lines: Hebrew geber — a strong man, a mighty man; the first element of the name.
Hebrew El — God, the Mighty One; the second element.
Together: “man of God” or “mighty one of God,” describing the angel’s strength as wholly God’s.
The name Gabrī’ēl appears in Daniel, and as Greek Gabriēl in Luke.
Michael (“who is like God?”) is the only other angel named in the canon.
usage: Gabriel’s annunciation to Mary is read every Advent as the herald of the incarnation.
His revelation of the seventy weeks to Daniel is a key text in Messianic chronology.
He is cited to correct both angel-veneration and the denial of the angelic ministry.

etymology: A translation of the explanation given for the name Eve, Hebrew Ḥawwāh, connected with ḥāy (living); “because she was the mother of all living.”
biblical_def: “The mother of all living” is the title Adam gave to his wife when he named her Eve, after the fall and after the first promise of the gospel. The name is a confession of faith in the face of the sentence of death: though God had said “dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return,” Adam looked upon his wife and named her Life, believing the LORD’s word that her seed should bruise the serpent’s head. Eve is the mother of all living in the plainest sense—every human being who has ever drawn breath descends from her, the one historical first mother of the whole race, so that all nations are of one blood. But the title carries also a redemptive note. Through the woman came sin, and through the woman, in the line of her seed, came the Saviour; the same Eve who first transgressed is the first to receive the promise of the One who would undo the transgression. The dictionary receives Eve as a real woman, the literal first mother of mankind, and reads her title as Adam’s early act of faith—naming life where God had pronounced death, because God had promised a Redeemer.
webster_summary: The title Adam gave to Eve after the fall, confessing her as the literal first mother of the whole human race and, in faith, the bearer of the promised seed.
webster_full: MOTHER OF ALL LIVING, the explanation Scripture gives for the name Eve.
Bestowed by Adam after the fall and after the first promise of a Redeemer.
Marks Eve as the one historical first mother from whom the whole race descends.
An act of faith, naming life where God had sentenced the man and woman to death.
Bound up with the promise that the woman’s seed should bruise the serpent’s head.
scriptures: Gen 3:20
And Adam called his wife’s name Eve; because she was the mother of all living.
Gen 3:15
And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.
And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;
For Adam was first formed, then Eve.
corruption_summary: Eve is reduced to myth or recast as victim-heroine, denying her historical motherhood of the race.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning corruption denies that Eve was a real woman and the literal first mother of all mankind, treating Genesis as a symbolic story of human origins rather than history. But the unity of the race in one first parent is the foundation of crucial doctrines: of one blood God made all nations, original sin is imputed because all sinned in Adam, and the incarnate Christ is the second Adam who recovers what the first lost. Dissolve the historical Eve and these doctrines lose their footing.

A second corruption inverts the narrative, casting Eve as a liberated heroine who reached for forbidden knowledge against a repressive God, and recasting her deception as awakening. Scripture is sober: “the woman being deceived was in the transgression.” Yet the dictionary refuses to make Eve a mere cautionary figure, for her title is gospel—the mother of all living is also, in the line of her seed, the mother through whom the Life of the world would come. Death entered by her hand; through her seed came the Author of life.
roots_summary: Her name Eve means “life,” and the title interprets it: she is the living source of all who live.
roots_lines: Hebrew Ḥawwāh — Eve, connected with the root for living, ḥāy.
Hebrew ḥay — living, alive; the same root in the word for “life.”
The phrase ’ēm kol-ḥāy — “mother of all living,” Adam’s explanation of the name.
Greek Zōē in the Septuagint renders Eve, meaning “Life.”
The naming follows the protoevangelium of Genesis 3:15, the first promise of the gospel.
usage: The title is cited to affirm the historical unity of the human race in one first mother.
Adam’s naming of Eve is preached as an early act of faith in the promised seed.
Eve’s motherhood undergirds the doctrines of original sin and of Christ as second Adam.
